variants.name: Core Data merge policy
variants.implementation_notes: Core Data's save is the commit-time validation: a conflict is the mismatch between the state at the context layer, the persistent-store coordinator cache and the external store, and it surfaces as an optimistic-locking failure (NSMergeConflict) when the context saves stale data. The context's NSMergePolicy decides what happens - NSMergePolicy.error (the default) surfaces the failure, mergeByPropertyObjectTrump/StoreTrump and overwrite/rollback resolve it automatically, and a custom policy can override resolve(optimisticLockingConflicts:). Core Data tracks the per-object version itself, so no token column has to be maintained in the model.
pitfalls: Trump and overwrite policies resolve conflicts silently in favour of one side - convenient, but they turn a detected conflict back into a lost update unless the direction is a conscious business rule.
A save can also fail for constraint (uniqueness) conflicts, which NSMergePolicy resolves through resolve(constraintConflicts:), so a single policy may not cover both paths.
Optimistic-locking failures also appear when more than one Core Data stack references the same external store, bypassing a stack's own version tracking.

variants.name: CloudKit record change tag
variants.implementation_notes: CloudKit applies the same validation one level up: every CKRecord carries a server-assigned record change tag, and saving a record whose tag is stale is rejected with CKError.Code.serverRecordChanged, whose userInfo carries the client, server and ancestor copies of the record. The app merges its changes into the server copy - Apple's documentation states that merging into either of the other copies conflicts again because they still hold the old record change tag - and saves that, which is exactly re-read-merge-retry with an opaque token.
pitfalls: Merging into the client or ancestor copy instead of the server copy raises serverRecordChanged again - both stale copies keep the old change tag.
The change tag is opaque and server-assigned: only a fetched record carries it, so a locally constructed record has no token to validate against.
The server copy's fields must be re-read before merging; writing the local fields wholesale over the server copy is last-writer-wins with extra steps.
